title: A Perceptual Assessment of the Physical Environment in Teaching Buildings and Its Influence on Students' Mental Well-Being
research_question: This article aims to evaluate students' perceptual assessments of different aspects of the physical environment within the school building. Additionally, it seeks to analyze the impact of these perceptual evaluations on students' “anxiety or not” (AON). It conducts cause profiling and proposes optimization strategies.

participants.description: College students (227 males, 213 females) from various grades (1st-4th year) at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University, Hangzhou, China. 107 (24.318%) reported anxiety.
participants.recruitment: In-person questionnaire survey and an online questionnaire hosted on the “Questionnaire Star” platform.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Building Two at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University, a U-shaped teaching building with an internal courtyard, semi-outdoor corridors, and classrooms. The study focused on the physical environment of the classroom area, semi-outdoor area, and courtyard area.

Perceptual evaluation of total physical environment factors

findings.mechanism: The authors interpret p=0.075 as significant at a 0.1 level, indicating an effect.
findings.quote: at a significance level of 0.1, the winter thermal comfort of semi-outdoor spaces (p = 0.075) significantly affects the occurrence of student anxiety.

mechanisms: Inadequate ventilation, lighting, noise, and thermal comfort create unsatisfactory physical conditions that exacerbate student anxiety.
Lack of perceived control over the physical environment (e.g., inability to improve conditions without compromising other aspects) is a fundamental cause of anxiety among students.
Exposure to natural features (landscape views, semi-outdoor areas) reduces stress through psychological and physiological means.
Overcrowding in indoor spaces (due to insufficient semi-outdoor areas) negatively impacts mood and increases anxiety.
High temperatures adversely affect mental health, potentially leading to depression and anxiety.
Natural light has antidepressant effects, and insufficient natural light in classrooms can increase the risk of anxiety.
moderators: Gender (male students being less likely to develop anxiety than female students)
Grade level (second-year students showing the highest anxiety rate, fourth-year students the lowest)
implementation_implications: Design and renovate academic buildings to enhance students' mental well-being by improving the physical environment.
Address unsuitable lighting near classroom windows through shading systems and innovative ceiling designs.
Implement balconies on the southern side of classrooms to shield from direct sunlight, moderate outdoor climate impact, and create semi-outdoor resting areas.

Enhance natural ventilation and thermal comfort, especially during seasons when air conditioning is unnecessary, by addressing issues related to inner corridor layouts (e.g., incorporating light wells).
Prioritize the creation of a favorable microclimate in courtyards by adjusting height-to-width ratio, increasing greenery, and providing adequate shading.
Ensure adequate semi-outdoor areas with good landscape views to prevent overcrowding, improve mood, and facilitate social interactions.

limitations: Study conducted exclusively in one specific teaching building at one university, limiting generalizability.
Data collection relied on questionnaires, which may be susceptible to extraneous influences and discrepancies between reported and actual psychological states.
Limited scope of the article and data collected, primarily focusing on the direct impact of independent variables on anxiety.

Potential variations in the relationship between physical environment factors and anxiety based on students' gender, socioeconomic status, or other demographic characteristics were not explored in depth.
Other environmental factors such as landscape design, vegetation types, architectural aesthetics and colors, and accessibility were not investigated.

paper_metadata.title: A Perceptual Assessment of the Physical Environment in Teaching Buildings and Its Influence on Students’ Mental Well-Being
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A Perceptual Assessment of the Physical Environment in Teaching Buildings and Its Influence on Students’ Mental Well-Being
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Numerous studies have examined the impact of the built environment on mental health, yet there remains an underexplored area concerning how microenvironments within educational buildings affect students’ mental well-being from a physical environment standpoint. This paper fills this gap by utilizing data from 440 valid questionnaires to develop regression models that assess students’ perceptions of physical environment factors in college teaching buildings and their impact on anxiety likelihood. This study examined the physical environment of the teaching building’s interior, courtyard, and semi-outdoor areas. Findings indicate that students’ perceptions of specific physical environment factors—such as classroom ventilation (p < 0.01, OR = 0.330), lighting (p < 0.01, OR = 0.444), noise conditions (p < 0.01, OR = 0.415), courtyard thermal comfort (p < 0.01, OR = 0.504), and the views from semi-outdoor areas (p < 0.01, OR = 2.779)—significantly influence the likelihood of experiencing anxiety. Optimal physical conditions are linked to reduced student anxiety. The suitability of the physical environment of teaching buildings is interrelated, and it is urgently necessary to address issues related to unsuitable lighting in window areas of classrooms, as well as problems with ventilation, lighting, and noise caused by the corridor layout within teaching buildings. These insights are crucial for the design and renovation of academic buildings to enhance students’ mental well-being.
